entries_new.name: Republic of Pirates at Nassau
entries_new.founder: Benjamin Hornigold and Henry Jennings, the leading rival captains
entries_new.stopped_by: Woodes Rogers, royal governor of the Bahamas
entries_new.pop: Over 1,000 pirates and about 100 inhabitants, per the Governor of Bermuda
entries_new.laws: An informal pirate code: crews voted on captains and shared plunder
entries_new.challenge: Great Britain: Captain Vincent Pearse of HMS Phoenix in 1717, then Woodes Rogers in 1718
entries_new.mechanism: Pirates moved into a town its government had abandoned and ran it under a shipboard code of votes and shared loot.
entries_new.story:
Nassau, on New Providence island in the Bahamas, was left without any English government after French and Spanish attacks in 1703 and 1706. From 1713 out-of-work privateers (private ships licensed to raid in wartime) used it as a pirate base. The Governor of Bermuda counted over 1,000 pirates against about a hundred townspeople.
It was never a formal republic. Crews followed a pirate code, voted captains in and out, and shared loot. Royal governor Woodes Rogers arrived in 1718 offering a pardon, hired the ex-pirate Benjamin Hornigold to hunt the holdouts, and nine men were executed on 12 December 1718.

entries_new.name: Libertalia
entries_new.founder: Captain James Misson, a figure known only from the 1724 book
entries_new.laws: Described only in the 1724 book: direct democracy, councils of delegates and goods held in common
entries_new.mechanism: None on record; the book describes a colony of pirates ruling themselves from a fortified harbour.
entries_new.story:
Libertalia, also spelled Libertatia, is a pirate colony said to have stood in Madagascar in the late 17th century under a Captain James Misson. Its only source is volume 2 of A General History of the Pyrates (1724), by Captain Charles Johnson, which describes direct democracy, shared wealth and two forts of 40 guns.
The consensus of modern scholarship is that it was not a real place. Real pirate settlements on and around Madagascar appear often in official letters of the period, while Libertalia appears only in Johnson. The Oxford Research Encyclopedia of African History calls it fictitious. Those real settlements may have inspired the story.
entries_new.anchor: Antsiranana Bay, northern Madagascar, the place named by legend; the book itself gives no firm location

entries_new.name: Baratarians of Barataria Bay
entries_new.mechanism: Smugglers used an island base the government could not easily reach, then bargained their fleet's help for a pardon.
entries_new.story:
Barataria Bay is a marshy bay on the Louisiana coast, cut off from the Gulf of Mexico by two barrier islands. After the Embargo Act of 1807 banned US foreign trade, the brothers Jean and Pierre Lafitte moved their smuggling business to an island there. By 1810 the port was thriving and had moved into piracy.
A US naval force invaded in September 1814 and captured most of the fleet. Lafitte and his men then helped General Andrew Jackson at the Battle of New Orleans in return for a legal pardon.

entries_new.name: Campeche colony on Galveston Island
entries_new.laws: Newcomers took an oath of loyalty to Lafitte
entries_new.mechanism: A pirate occupied a thinly governed island outside US authority and gave his raiders forged papers from a nation that did not exist.
entries_new.story:
In 1817 the pirate Jean Lafitte took command of Galveston Island in Spanish Texas and named his colony Campeche. He was also working as a paid spy for Spain. His men built 200 houses, newcomers swore an oath of loyalty to him, and he forged letters of marque (licences to raid ships) from an imaginary nation. The colony grew to 100 to 200 men and several women.
A September 1818 hurricane left only six houses habitable. In 1821 the USS Enterprise came after one of his captains attacked an American ship, and Lafitte left on 7 May without a fight. His men burned the settlement.

entries_new.name: Republic of Salé
entries_new.pop: About 3,000 Moriscos from Hornachos, then about 10,000 more after 1609
entries_new.laws: Council (Diwan) electing a governor each May
entries_new.challenge: Moroccan sultans; the Zawiya Dila'iya from 1641; English bombardment in 1637
entries_new.recognition: England negotiated a treaty with its ally; Dutch and French consuls resided there
entries_new.mechanism: Refugees with a raiding fleet threw out the sultan's governor and ran the port through an elected council.
entries_new.story:
The Republic of Salé was a corsair city-state (a base for sea raiders) at the mouth of the Bou Regreg river in Morocco, founded by Moriscos, Muslims expelled from Spain. In April 1627 settlers from Hornachos expelled the sultan's governor and stopped paying his tithe. A council of 12 to 14 notables, later 16, elected a governor each May.
The English diplomat John Harrison negotiated a treaty with their ally Sidi al-Ayachi in May 1627, and the Dutch and French later posted consuls there. Its fleets raided as far as Iceland and held Lundy in the Bristol Channel for five years. Sultan Moulay al-Rashid ended its independence in June 1668.

entries_new.name: Pirate base at Île Sainte-Marie
entries_new.mechanism: Former pirates set up trading posts on an island no European state held, close to rich shipping lanes.
entries_new.story:
Île Sainte-Marie, now Nosy Boraha, is an island 60 km long off the east coast of Madagascar. It served as a pirate base from Adam Baldridge's arrival in 1691 until John Pro in 1719, near the routes of ships returning from the East Indies. William Kidd, Henry Every and Thomas Tew are among those said to have lived on an islet in the bay of Ambodifotatra. Baldridge, a former pirate, founded a trading post there.
Rumours placed a pirate kingdom under Every there. The Betsimisaraka ruler ceded the island to France in 1750, and islanders killed the French colonists in 1752.

entries_new.name: Tortuga and the Brethren of the Coast
entries_new.stopped_by: Spain repeatedly, then absorption by the French West India Company
entries_new.mechanism: Buccaneers kept returning to a small island Spain would not garrison for long, then sold it to a French company.
entries_new.story:
Tortuga is an island of 180 square km off northern Haiti. French and English settlers used it as a buccaneer base from 1630 and, by 1641, called themselves the Brethren of the Coast. Spain attacked and expelled them in 1635, 1638 and 1654, and each time they came back.
The pirates never really controlled the island. From 1655 an English governor, Elias Watts, held a commission from Jamaica, and in 1664 the French buccaneer Jeremie Dechamps sold it for 15,000 livres to the French West India Company. The colony's capital moved to the mainland in 1676, and an English law of 1680 and the Treaty of Ratisbon of 1684 cut away the legal cover for raiding.

entries_new.name: Pirates of Leamcon, Munster
entries_new.mechanism: Pirates used a remote coast and a legal loophole that made prosecution difficult.
entries_new.story: In the early 17th century Leamcon, near Schull on the coast of Munster in southern Ireland, was a pirate stronghold, and pirates traded openly in nearby Baltimore and on Whiddy Island. The province was hard to control from London or Dublin. Literate pirates could escape secular trial until 1613 by pleading benefit of clergy, an old rule that sent clergy to church courts. Munster worked as a summer alternative to the Moroccan base of Mehdya.

entries_new.name: Mehdya (La Mamora)
entries_new.mechanism: Pirates used a harbour outside effective state control, moving away in the season when anti-piracy galleys could operate.
entries_new.story: Mehdya, also called La Mamora, on the Atlantic coast of Morocco, was a pirate haven in the early 17th century. It worked as a seasonal partner to the coast of Munster in Ireland: in summer Mehdya became less safe, because calmer water favoured the galleys sent to suppress piracy. Sources on pirate havens list it with Salé, Algiers and Tunis among the Barbary corsair bases.

entries_new.name: Ghar al Milh (Porto Farina)
entries_new.mechanism: A harbour used as a base by North African corsairs.
entries_new.story: Ghar al Milh, called Porto Farina by Europeans, is a harbour on the north coast of Tunisia listed as a notable base for Barbary corsairs, the sea raiders of North Africa, who operated from the 16th to the 19th century. Those raiders attacked European shipping and enslaved thousands of captives. The United States fought the First and Second Barbary Wars (1801 to 1805, and 1815) to end the threat to its ships.

entries_new.name: Zheng Yi Sao's pirate confederation
entries_new.founder: Zheng Yi and Zheng Yi Sao
entries_new.stopped_by: Portuguese navy defeats, then a negotiated surrender to the Qing
entries_new.pop: About 400 junks and 40,000 to 70,000 pirates in 1805
entries_new.laws: A signed confederation agreement of July 1805
entries_new.challenge: Qing China and Portugal at Macau
entries_new.recognition: The Qing negotiated her surrender and pardoned her
entries_new.mechanism: Rival pirate fleets signed an agreement giving up some of their independence, then used their size to bargain for a pardon.
entries_new.story: The Chinese pirate leader Shi Yang, known as Zheng Yi Sao or Ching Shih, ran a confederation of six flag-coloured fleets in the South China Sea. Her husband Zheng Yi had united the rival pirate groups by a signed agreement in July 1805, when the fleet had about 400 junks and 40,000 to 70,000 pirates. She took over after he died on 16 November 1807. After defeats by the Portuguese navy, she negotiated a surrender to Qing officials in 1810 that let her and Zhang Bao keep 24 ships and over 1,400 pirates and avoid prosecution.

entries_new.name: Port Royal, Jamaica
entries_new.mechanism: A colonial government licensed raiders against Spain, and pirates used the port it offered.
entries_new.story: Port Royal stands at the mouth of Kingston Harbour in Jamaica. England captured it in 1655, and by the later 17th century it was the shipping centre of the Caribbean and home port to English and Dutch government-sponsored privateers encouraged to attack Spanish ships. Pirates gathered there from as far as Madagascar, and folklore called it the wickedest city on Earth. It stayed under the English Crown throughout, with five forts by 1692. An earthquake and tsunami destroyed it on 7 June 1692, which led to the founding of Kingston.

entries_new.name: Victual Brothers on Gotland
entries_new.laws: The later name Likedeelers means equal sharers
entries_new.mechanism: Privateers kept their ships and crews after their war contract and seized an island to operate from.
entries_new.story: The Victual Brothers were privateers hired in 1392 by the Dukes of Mecklenburg to carry supplies to besieged Stockholm during a war with Queen Margaret of Denmark. They turned to piracy, and Baltic trade virtually collapsed. In 1394 they took over the island of Gotland, with the port of Visby as a listed haven. The Teutonic Order drove them out in 1398. The survivors, calling themselves the Likedeelers (equal sharers), raided as far as France and Spain and hit Bergen in 1429.

entries_new.name: Cilician pirates
entries_new.pop: Tens of thousands of pirates; 1,000 ships per Plutarch
entries_new.mechanism: Pirates held a rugged coast and fortified anchorages when no strong naval power was left in the Mediterranean.
entries_new.story: Cilician pirates dominated the Mediterranean from the 2nd century BC, based on the southern coast of modern Turkey, with Coracesium as their main base. Carthage had been destroyed, and Rome had a small navy that it hired as needed. Plutarch claimed they had over 1,000 ships and captured 400 towns. They ransomed towns and kidnapped rich people, and the source counts tens of thousands of pirates. Pompey suppressed them in 67 to 66 BC. The source describes no single government of theirs.

entries_new.name: Abraham Samuel at Fort Dauphin
entries_new.mechanism: A shipwrecked pirate took a leading position in a local kingdom and ran a mixed force from an abandoned fort.
entries_new.story: Abraham Samuel, a pirate quartermaster thought to have been of mixed African and European ancestry, was wrecked in a storm in October 1697 in the harbour of the abandoned French settlement of Fort Dauphin (modern Tôlanaro) in Madagascar. From then until his death there in 1705 he led a combined force of pirates and the Antanosy kingdom, under the names Deaan Tuley-Noro and Tolinar Rex. Fort Dauphin appears on lists of Madagascan pirate havens.

entries_new.name: Kingdom of Tungning
entries_new.challenge: Dutch East India Company, then Qing China
entries_new.mechanism: A sea-trading family with a fleet expelled a colonial power from an island and ruled there in the name of a fallen dynasty.
entries_new.story: The Kingdom of Tungning was a maritime state that ruled part of southwestern Taiwan and the Penghu islands from 1662 to 1683. Its founder was Zheng Chenggong, known as Koxinga, son of the former pirate turned general Zheng Zhilong and a loyalist of China's fallen Ming dynasty. He attacked the Dutch fortress in 1661 and drove the Dutch from Taiwan. At its height its ships held major sea lanes and traded from Japan to Southeast Asia. It remained a Ming loyalist base until the Qing dynasty annexed it in 1683.

entries_new.name: Hobyo, Somalia
entries_new.challenge: International naval patrols and Somali authorities
entries_new.mechanism: Pirates worked from a port where the national government could not enforce the law of the sea.
entries_new.story: Hobyo is an old port in the Mudug region of central Somalia, founded as a coastal outpost in the 13th century. In the early 2000s it was listed among modern pirate havens, at a time when Somalia's Transitional Federal Government was believed unable to enforce maritime law. A 2017 report described Mohamed Garfanje's Hobyo-Haradhere Piracy Network as working with the Islamic State group in Somalia. The sources read describe no pirate government there.

sources.t: Piracy off the coast of Somalia

entries_new.name: Harardhere, Somalia
entries_new.stopped_by: Al-Shabaab took the town by 2012; Somali Armed Forces retook it in 2023
entries_new.mechanism: Investors funded attacks through a local exchange in a town outside government control.
entries_new.story: Harardhere is a town in the Mudug province of Somalia, listed among modern pirate havens in the early 2000s. Wikipedia's article on Somali piracy describes a stock exchange in the town where investors bought and sold shares in upcoming attacks, with ransoms delivered in US dollar bills in sacks. The armed group al-Shabaab controlled the town from at least 2012 until the Somali Armed Forces retook it on 16 January 2023.

sources.t: Piracy off the coast of Somalia

entries_new.name: Eyl, Puntland
entries_new.stopped_by: Puntland military forces and community initiatives
entries_new.mechanism: Armed fishermen turned to holding ships for ransom from a remote coastal town.
entries_new.story: Eyl is an old port town in the Nugal region of Puntland, Somalia, which also served as a capital of the Dervish State from 1905 to 1908. Illegal foreign fishing off its coast led fishermen to band together, and piracy grew from that. It became listed as a pirate haven in the early 2000s. In April 2009 pirates seized the MV Maersk Alabama 240 nautical miles southeast of the town. By 2010 Puntland's military and community efforts had forced the pirates out of their operating centres in the area.

sources.t: Piracy off the coast of Somalia

entries_new.name: Uskoks of Senj
entries_new.mechanism: Unpaid border soldiers used a Habsburg fort as a base to raid shipping.
entries_new.story: The Uskoks were irregular soldiers on the eastern Adriatic coast who fought the Ottomans from small fast rowing boats. Since they were rarely paid their annual subsidy, they turned to piracy. They settled first at the fortress of Klis under captain Petar Kružić and then at Senj, inside the Habsburg Military Frontier, the border zone the Habsburgs ran as a military district. Their raids helped renew war between Venice and the Ottomans in 1570 to 1573. After the Uskok War of 1615 to 1618 their activity at Senj mostly ceased, and they were disbanded.

entries_new.name: HMS Bounty mutineers on Pitcairn
entries_new.founder: Fletcher Christian and eight other mutineers, with Tahitian men and women
entries_new.challenge: Britain took the island in as a colony and later prosecuted islanders for sexual assault
entries_new.recognition: Became a British colony; never separately recognised
entries_new.mechanism: Mutineers settled on a remote island and burned their ship.
entries_new.story:
In 1789 acting lieutenant Fletcher Christian led a mutiny on HMS Bounty, a British naval ship sent under William Bligh to carry breadfruit plants. In 1790 nine mutineers, six Tahitian men, 11 women and a baby girl settled on Pitcairn Island in the South Pacific and set fire to the ship. The article also gives twelve Tahitian women as ancestors.
No ship landed for years. Islanders date British colony status to 30 November 1838, when women also gained the vote. Pitcairn remains a British Overseas Territory, with 35 permanent residents in 2023. Abuse allegations uncovered in 1999 led to a high-profile sexual assault trial in 2004.

entries_new.name: Battleship Potemkin mutiny
entries_new.stopped_by: Lack of supplies, then Romanian asylum terms
entries_new.challenge: Imperial Russian Navy Black Sea Fleet
entries_new.mechanism: Sailors took a warship and ran it through an elected committee, hoping the rest of the fleet would join them.
entries_new.story: The crew of the Russian battleship Potemkin mutinied in the Black Sea in June 1905, during the Revolution of 1905. They killed seven officers, formed a ship's committee and raised a red flag at Odessa, where a general strike was under way, but refused to land men to help take the city. The first squadron sent to force surrender turned away. Short of food, water and coal, the crew reached Constanța, Romania, at 23:00 on 7 July. Romania gave asylum on condition that they disarm and hand over the ship, and Russia recovered it.
entries_new.anchor: Constanța, Romania, where the mutiny ended

entries_new.name: Santa Maria hijacking
entries_new.stopped_by: US Navy pressure, then surrender to Brazil for asylum
entries_new.pop: 24 activists with Galvão, 600 passengers and 300 crew
entries_new.recognition: Brazil gave the rebels political asylum
entries_new.mechanism: Rebels seized a liner at sea, intending to use it to reach Angola and declare a rival government there.
entries_new.story:
On 22 January 1961, Portuguese and Spanish rebels led by the exiled officer Henrique Galvão seized the Santa Maria, a Portuguese passenger liner, in the Atlantic. Galvão later said he meant to sail to Angola and set up a rebel government against the dictator Salazar. A US Navy force surrounded the ship off Recife. On 2 February Galvão and his 24 activists handed the ship, 600 passengers and 300 crew to Brazil in exchange for asylum.
US legal experts could not support a finding of piracy, because the seizure was political, not for private ends. The United States treated Galvão as an insurgent, though one US naval writer argued it should have called him a pirate.
entries_new.anchor: Recife, Brazil, where the hijacking ended

sources.t: Piracy: A Modern Conspectus (US Naval Institute Proceedings, 1965)

entries_new.name: Batavia mutineers on Beacon Island
entries_new.stopped_by: Wiebbe Hayes and his soldiers, then Commander Pelsaert
entries_new.laws: None recorded; Dutch East India Company court tried them
entries_new.mechanism: Mutineers seized power over shipwreck survivors by killing them, on islands far from any authority.
entries_new.story: The Dutch East India ship Batavia struck a reef in the Houtman Abrolhos islands off western Australia on 4 June 1629. Commander Francisco Pelsaert left in a longboat to get help. The official left in charge, Jeronimus Cornelisz, had been plotting a mutiny before the wreck. With other mutineers he took over the survivors and had about 125 people murdered, including women and children. Soldiers under Wiebbe Hayes, sent off to die, found water and fought back. Pelsaert returned in October, tried and convicted Cornelisz and six men, and had them executed.
entries_new.anchor: Beacon Island, Houtman Abrolhos, Western Australia

entries_new.name: Whaleship Globe mutiny and Mili Atoll
entries_new.stopped_by: His fellow mutineers, who shot him
entries_new.mechanism: A mutineer planned to set himself up as ruler on a remote inhabited atoll, using the seized ship.
entries_new.story: On 26 January 1824, near Fanning Island in the Pacific, the crew of the Nantucket whaler Globe mutinied and killed their officers. The instigator was the harpooner Samuel Comstock, aged 22. On 14 February they brought the ship to Mili Atoll, an inhabited atoll, where Comstock wanted to create his own kingdom. Other mutineers suspected he meant to destroy the ship and kill the rest of the crew, and Silas Payne, John Oliver and two others shot him. Gilbert Smith and five others then cut the cable and sailed away, and the ship returned to its owners.

entries_new.name: HMS Hermione mutiny
entries_new.mechanism: Mutineers killed the officers and handed the ship to a rival government in place of keeping it.
entries_new.story: HMS Hermione was a 32-gun British frigate. While it was operating in the Caribbean in 1797 part of the crew mutinied, killing the captain, eight other officers, two midshipmen and a clerk, then surrendered the ship to the Spanish authorities. It is recorded as the bloodiest mutiny in Royal Navy history.

entries_new.name: Guaymas Mutiny
entries_new.mechanism: Sailors took a government gunboat during a civil war.
entries_new.story: On 22 February 1914, during the Mexican Revolution, Mexican Navy sailors under Lieutenant Hilario Rodríguez Malpica seized the gunboat Tampico off Guaymas, Mexico. The seizure led to a naval campaign off Topolobampo. The sailors were taking a side in a civil war, using a government warship.

entries_new.name: Vlieter Incident
entries_new.mechanism: Sailors refused to fight and surrendered a squadron to an invading power.
entries_new.story: The Vlieter Incident was a mutiny in 1799 in a fleet squadron of the Batavian Republic, the state that then governed the Netherlands. It caused the squadron to be surrendered to the British without a fight at the start of the Anglo-Russian invasion of Holland.

entries_new.name: 1936 Naval Revolt, Portugal
entries_new.mechanism: Sailors held their officers and tried to take two warships out of the government's reach.
entries_new.story: The 1936 Naval Revolt in Portugal is also called the Mutiny on the Tagus ships. Sailors aboard two Portuguese ships imprisoned their officers and tried to sail out into the open sea. Coastal artillery disabled both ships. Shortly afterwards the Estado Novo, the authoritarian government of the time, founded the Portuguese Legion, a state militia. No territory or government came out of it.

entries_new.name: Wager Mutiny
entries_new.founder: The main body of the crew
entries_new.challenge: Captain David Cheap and the Admiralty
entries_new.mechanism: Shipwrecked sailors threw off their captain's command on an island far from any government, then left it.
entries_new.story: HMS Wager, a British warship in a squadron bound to attack Spanish interests in the Pacific, lost contact while rounding Cape Horn and was wrecked in 1741 on a desolate island off southern Chile, later named Wager Island. Most of the crew mutinied against Captain David Cheap, left him with a group of loyal men on the island, and set off in a modified schooner, the Speedwell, through the Strait of Magellan toward Portuguese-held territory. The Admiralty later investigated the loss of the ship.

entries_new.name: La Amistad revolt
entries_new.challenge: Spanish owners and the United States
entries_new.recognition: US Supreme Court restored their freedom
entries_new.mechanism: Captives took over the ship carrying them and tried to sail it, then won their freedom in a US court.
entries_new.story: In July 1839, 53 Mende captives, including four children, rose against the crew of the schooner La Amistad, which was carrying them along the coast of Cuba, and killed the captain. Their leader Sengbe Pieh ordered the two owners to sail to Africa. The owners steered north instead, and the revenue cutter Washington seized the ship off Long Island, New York. They were jailed in New Haven on charges including murder and piracy. In United States v. The Amistad (1841) the US Supreme Court decided in favour of the Mende and restored their freedom.

entries_new.name: Revolt of the Lash
entries_new.mechanism: Sailors mutinied in the capital's harbour and pressed Congress into passing a law.
entries_new.story: The Revolt of the Lash was a naval mutiny in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, in late November 1910, against the whipping of Afro-Brazilian and mixed-race sailors by white officers. Crewmen of the new battleship Minas Geraes had planned it for years, and the experienced sailor João Cândido led it. Congress, led by Senator Rui Barbosa, sent a former navy captain as go-between and passed a bill that gave amnesty to all involved and ended corporal punishment. No separate territory came of it.

entries_new.name: Storozhevoy mutiny
entries_new.mechanism: An officer seized a warship with the aim of broadcasting a political demand from it.
entries_new.story: In November 1975 the political officer Valery Sablin took control of the Soviet frigate Storozhevoy, based in the Baltic. He lured the captain below on 9 November, then won over the 145 to 155 sailors with a speech, and planned to steam to Leningrad and broadcast his revolutionary message. Moscow feared he might seek asylum in Sweden and sent thirteen naval vessels and 60 warplanes after him. Aircraft bombed near the ship and strafed it until the steering failed. Only Sablin and seaman Alexander Shein were tried and convicted.

entries_new.name: SS Columbia Eagle incident
entries_new.recognition: Cambodia first granted, then withdrew, asylum
entries_new.mechanism: Two sailors took a cargo ship by threat and sailed it to a country they hoped would shelter them.
entries_new.story: In March 1970 two crew members of the US merchant ship Columbia Eagle seized it with a bomb threat and handguns. The ship was carrying napalm bombs for the US Air Force in the Vietnam War. They forced 24 crew into lifeboats in the Gulf of Thailand and made the rest sail to a bay near Sihanoukville, Cambodia. They asked Cambodia for political asylum, which was first granted, but they were later arrested and jailed.

entries_new.name: Kiel mutiny
entries_new.founder: Sailors of the High Seas Fleet
entries_new.mechanism: Sailors refused orders, took a naval port and ran it through elected councils.
entries_new.story: The Kiel mutiny broke out on 3 November 1918 among sailors of the German High Seas Fleet, after crews at Wilhelmshaven refused on 30 October to sail for a final battle against the British Grand Fleet. The Admiralty had ordered the battle without the government's knowledge. The mutineers took over Kiel through workers' and soldiers' councils and spread the councils across Germany. Within days the revolution swept aside the Hohenzollern monarchy.

entries_new.name: Paris Commune
entries_new.stopped_by: French Army under the Third Republic
entries_new.pop: Council of 92 members, one for every 20,000 residents
entries_new.laws: Separation of church and state, remission of rent, abolition of child labour
entries_new.challenge: French Third Republic under Adolphe Thiers
entries_new.mechanism: An armed city militia held the capital and ran it through an elected council, refusing the national government.
entries_new.story:
The Paris Commune was a revolutionary government that seized power in Paris on 18 March 1871, after France lost the war with Prussia. National Guard soldiers took the city, killed two army generals and refused the authority of the Third Republic. Elections on 26 March chose a council of 92 members.
It separated church and state, cancelled rents and banned child labour. The national army retook the city in the Bloody Week from 21 to 28 May. Government forces killed or executed an estimated 10,000 to 15,000 Communards, with one unconfirmed 1876 estimate of 20,000. The Commune executed the Archbishop of Paris and about one hundred hostages.

entries_new.name: Korean People's Association in Manchuria
entries_new.pop: Two million Korean refugees, as described by its Wikipedia article
entries_new.laws: Village assemblies and a federation of councils
entries_new.challenge: Korean communists and the Empire of Japan
entries_new.mechanism: Refugees built councils, banks and schools in a region where warlords and foreign powers competed for control.
entries_new.story: The Korean People's Association in Manchuria, also called Shinmin, was a self-governing area in Manchuria from August 1929 to September 1931, described as home to two million Korean refugees from Japanese rule. Korean anarchists and nationalists set it up to provide food, schools and self-defence. Village assemblies made most decisions, with councils at village, district and regional level, and it ran mutual banks and cooperatives. Korean communists assassinated its military commander Kim Chwa-chin on 20 January 1930, and the Japanese invasion of Manchuria ended it.
entries_new.anchor: Hailin, Manchuria, China, where the founding Korean Anarchist Federation was set up

entries_new.name: Revolutionary Catalonia
entries_new.founder: CNT, FAI, UGT, POUM and PSUC
entries_new.stopped_by: Barcelona May Days, then the Nationalist victory in 1939
entries_new.challenge: Civil guards and the PSUC; Nationalist forces
entries_new.mechanism: Unions took factories and formed militias while a legal regional government kept its formal position.
entries_new.story: From 21 July 1936 to 8 May 1937, during the Spanish Civil War, trade unions and militias controlled most of the economy and armed forces of Catalonia in northeast Spain. The anarchist CNT union was the largest. The official Catalan government, the Generalitat, stayed in place, so there were two powers side by side. In the May Days of 1937 fighting broke out in Barcelona when civil guards tried to take a CNT-run telephone building. The communist PSUC replaced the CNT as the main force until Nationalist forces defeated them in 1939.

entries_new.name: Bavarian Soviet Republic
entries_new.challenge: Free State of Bavaria under Hoffmann and the German Army
entries_new.mechanism: Revolutionaries declared a council state in a regional capital after the elected government left for another city.
entries_new.story: Communists and anarchists declared the Bavarian Soviet Republic, a short-lived and unrecognised state centred on Munich, on 6 April 1919 during the German revolution. The Free State's government fled to Bamberg. The first leaders, under the playwright Ernst Toller, were ousted after six days by a Communist Party takeover led by Eugen Leviné, who put factories under worker control. Food shortages caused unrest. The German Army and 20,000 Freikorps paramilitaries broke through Munich's defences on 1 May and ended it on 3 May. Some 600 people died in the fighting.

entries_new.name: Hungarian Soviet Republic
entries_new.stopped_by: Romanian Army and the Allied blockade
entries_new.challenge: Romania, Czechoslovakia and the Allied powers
entries_new.mechanism: Communists and socialists took over an existing government and concentrated power in governing councils.
entries_new.story: The Hungarian Soviet Republic was a communist and socialist state from 21 March to August 1919, run through governing councils with Béla Kun as its main figure. At the start it held about 60% of the former Hungarian territory. It could not reach agreement with the Allied powers, which kept up an economic blockade, and fought Czechoslovak and Romanian forces. A Hungarian offensive against Romanian lines on the Tisza river from 20 July failed. Kun and most of the government fled to Vienna, a Social Democratic government took over on 1 August, and Romanian troops entered Budapest on 4 August.

entries_new.name: Limerick Soviet
entries_new.currency: Strike money printed by the committee
entries_new.challenge: British Army under the Defence of the Realm Act
entries_new.mechanism: A general strike committee took over food supply, prices and money for a city under military restrictions.
entries_new.story: The Limerick Soviet ran the Irish city of Limerick from 14 to 27 April 1919, at the start of the Irish War of Independence. The Limerick Trades and Labour Council called a general strike against a British Army order making the city a Special Military Area. A strike committee printed its own money, which local businesses accepted, set food prices and published newspapers. Dublin showed some sympathy, while the Belfast industrial area did not, and the National Union of Railwaymen gave no help.

entries_new.name: Strandzha Commune
entries_new.mechanism: Armed rebels attacked local Ottoman garrisons while villagers organised themselves in the mountains.
entries_new.story: The Strandzha Commune, also called the Strandzha Republic, was a short-lived anarchist commune in the mountains of East Thrace, then in the Ottoman Empire. Rebels of the revolutionary group IMARO proclaimed it during the Preobrazhenie Uprising, which began on 19 August 1903 when Mihail Gerdzhikov's militia marched on the port of Vasiliko. Local peasants organised communal life. The system lasted until 3 September, with some parts holding out another week, before the Ottoman army broke it up.

entries_new.name: Canton Commune
entries_new.founder: Zhang Tailei and Ye Ting, for the Chinese Communist Party
entries_new.challenge: National Revolutionary Army under the Kuomintang
entries_new.mechanism: Communists tried to win over local soldiers, take the city and declare a soviet, or workers' council government.
entries_new.story: The Canton Commune was the name given to a failed communist uprising in Guangzhou (Canton), southern China, in December 1927. Under Soviet pressure, the Chinese Communist Party launched it with a Revolutionary Military Council and renamed the city's political structure the Soviet of Workers, Soldiers and Peasant Deputies. National Revolutionary Army troops, 15,000 of them in the area, moved in and pushed the rebels back. It lasted only a short time. The article gives more than 5,700 communists dead and an equal number missing.

entries_new.name: Shanghai People's Commune
entries_new.founder: Zhang Chunqiao, Wang Hongwen and Yao Wenyuan
entries_new.challenge: The Shanghai Municipal Committee of Chen Pixian, Wei Wenbo and Cao Diqiu
entries_new.mechanism: Rebel factions backed by national leaders replaced a city government with a body modelled on the Paris Commune.
entries_new.story: The Shanghai People's Commune was created on 5 February 1967 during the Cultural Revolution in China, after Maoist rebels overthrew the city's party committee in the January Storm, a coup under the direction of the Cultural Revolution Group. Its leaders, including Zhang Chunqiao, modelled it on the Paris Commune and planned direct democracy for the city. National leaders including Mao Zedong backed the coup. The commune collapsed within 18 days after Mao withdrew his support, and a revolutionary committee of soldiers, cadres and rebels replaced it.

entries_new.name: Morelos Commune
entries_new.stopped_by: Assassination of Zapata in 1919, then a negotiated peace with Obregón
entries_new.laws: Plan of Ayala, written by Otilio Montaño
entries_new.challenge: Governments of Díaz, Madero, Huerta and Carranza
entries_new.mechanism: A guerrilla army held its home state and redistributed land under its own plan.
entries_new.story: The Morelos Commune was the area of southern Mexico run by Emiliano Zapata's Liberation Army of the South during the Mexican Revolution. The force fought four national governments from 1911 to 1920 to reclaim communal lands taken by big estates, under Zapata's Plan of Ayala, which called for land to be taken and given to peasants. After Zapata and Pancho Villa parted, the Zapatistas fortified themselves and focused on creating the commune. Zapata was assassinated in 1919. After the Carranza government fell, his successor Gildardo Magaña negotiated peace with President Álvaro Obregón.

entries_new.name: Gwangju Uprising
entries_new.mechanism: Citizens armed themselves from police armouries and ran the city through committees while negotiating with the army.
entries_new.story: In May 1980 students in Gwangju, South Korea, protested against martial law under the military ruler Chun Doo-hwan, and soldiers fired on them. Some citizens took up arms, formed militias, raided police stations and armouries, and took control of large sections of the city. Settlement Committees of citizens then split between surrender and continued resistance. The military retook the city. The government claimed 165 dead, while scholarship today estimates about 600 to 2,300.

entries_new.name: Oaxaca rebellion, 2006
entries_new.founder: Teachers' union and Popular Assembly of the Peoples of Oaxaca
entries_new.challenge: Governor Ulises Ruiz Ortiz and the Mexican federal government
entries_new.mechanism: Teachers and allied groups pushed police out of a state capital and ran it through mass assemblies.
entries_new.story: In May 2006 police in the Mexican state of Oaxaca opened fire on a protest by striking teachers. The dispute grew into a movement of the Popular Assembly of the Peoples of Oaxaca (APPO), which occupied the state capital and demanded that Governor Ulises Ruiz Ortiz resign, accusing him of corruption and repression. The conflict lasted over seven months with at least seventeen deaths. APPO held large assemblies and the article describes a citywide anarchist community lasting several months. President Vicente Fox sent federal police in October 2006 to retake the city. Human rights monitors accused the government of death squads.

entries_new.name: Republic of Ezo
entries_new.pop: A force of 4,000 troops took Hakodate
entries_new.laws: Government structure based on the United States, with samurai-only suffrage
entries_new.mechanism: A defeated navy sailed to a northern island, held an election and sought foreign recognition.
entries_new.story: The Republic of Ezo was a separatist state on the island now called Hokkaido, set up by part of the defeated Tokugawa shogunate's forces under Admiral Enomoto Takeaki. They captured Hakodate in December 1868. In an election limited to the samurai class, using open ballots, they chose Enomoto as president, the first election held in Japan. They approached foreign legations seeking recognition, and French officers including Jules Brunet served with them. An imperial force of 7,000 men won the Battle of Hakodate, and Enomoto surrendered on 26 June 1869.

entries_new.name: Kronstadt rebellion
entries_new.pop: About fifteen thousand at the 1 March assembly
entries_new.mechanism: A naval garrison used its island fortress to hold out against the government and press demands.
entries_new.story: For sixteen days in March 1921, sailors, naval infantry and civilians in Kronstadt, the Baltic Fleet base on Kotlin Island near Petrograd, rebelled against the Bolshevik government they had helped to establish. Led by Stepan Petrichenko, they passed a resolution with fifteen demands, and about fifteen thousand people attended an assembly on 1 March. After an ultimatum on 5 March, Bolshevik forces raided the island several times and suppressed the revolt on 18 March, shooting and imprisoning several thousand rebels. The political demands were not met. The crisis helped speed the New Economic Policy.

entries_new.name: Kingdom of Eunus in Sicily
entries_new.mechanism: Enslaved people seized cities and set up a kingdom with its own king and army.
entries_new.story: In 135 BC Eunus, a slave from Syria who claimed to be a prophet, captured the city of Enna in Sicily with 400 fellow slaves and proclaimed himself king under the name Antiochus. Cleon, another slave, stormed Agrigentum and became his military commander. They took Catana and Tauromenium and repelled several Roman attempts to end the revolt. The consul Publius Rupilius arrived in 134 and besieged the slave-held cities. The revolt ended in 132 with the fall of Enna and Tauromenium.

entries_new.name: Zanj Rebellion
entries_new.mechanism: Enslaved marsh workers and others held territory in southern Iraq while the Caliphate was weak from civil conflict.
entries_new.story: The Zanj Rebellion was a revolt against the Abbasid Caliphate from 869 to 883, begun near Basra in southern Iraq and led by Ali ibn Muhammad. It involved enslaved and freed Africans brought to drain the salt marshes, and grew to include others. Basra fell in September 871 after a blockade and was burned, with its people massacred. By 879 rebels had come within fifty miles of Baghdad. The revolt ended with the fall of its base al-Mukhtarah in August 883 and the death or capture of its leaders, after tens of thousands of deaths.

entries_new.name: Quilombo dos Palmares
entries_new.founder: Escaped slaves; later Ganga Zumba and Zumbi
entries_new.stopped_by: Army under Domingos Jorge Velho and Bernardo Vieira de Melo
entries_new.mechanism: Escaped slaves built fortified settlements in the interior and bargained with the colonial government while fighting it.
entries_new.story: Palmares was a community of escaped slaves and others in colonial Brazil, in today's state of Alagoas, from 1605 to 1694. Indigenous people lived there too. One estimate gives about 20,000 people in the 1690s, and Stuart Schwartz gives about 11,000. It had a king, Ganga Zumba, with officials and judges. After an attack in 1676 to 1677 he accepted the Pernambuco governor's offer of pardon, in return for moving closer to Portuguese settlements and giving back people not born in Palmares. His leader Zumbi refused. Six Portuguese expeditions failed between 1680 and 1686, and an army under Domingos Jorge Velho ended it in 1694.

entries_new.name: Makhnovshchina (Free Territory)
entries_new.laws: Regional Congress of Peasants, Workers and Insurgents; Military Revolutionary Council
entries_new.challenge: Austro-German forces, White forces and the Red Army
entries_new.mechanism: A peasant army held a region and organised it through congresses and free soviets, or local councils.
entries_new.story: The Makhnovshchina was a mass movement for anarchist communism during the Ukrainian War of Independence, named after Nestor Makhno, commander of the Revolutionary Insurgent Army. It began with farming communes in his home town of Huliaipole after the February Revolution of 1917. After a victory at Dibrivka it controlled much of Katerynoslav province, with a Regional Congress of Peasants, Workers and Insurgents and a Military Revolutionary Council. The Red Army invaded in January 1920. After a brief truce, the Starobilsk agreement, it attacked again and defeated the movement by August 1921.

entries_new.name: Regional Defence Council of Aragon
entries_new.challenge: Second Spanish Republic and the Communist Party of Spain
entries_new.mechanism: Anarchist militia and unions ran a region directly during a civil war, then sought a place within the Republic.
entries_new.story: The Regional Defence Council of Aragon was set up in October 1936 by anarchists of the CNT union during the Spanish Civil War, and it ran the eastern half of Aragon in northeast Spain. It controlled prices to limit inflation. It was the first autonomous government of Aragon since 1707, and from December 1936 included the other anti-fascist parties of the Popular Front. The Spanish Republic's authorities, pressed by the Communist Party of Spain, dissolved it in less than a year.

entries_new.name: Qarmatian state of al-Ahsa
entries_new.mechanism: A militant religious movement took a region at the edge of two rival caliphates and extracted tribute from both.
entries_new.story: The Qarmatians were an Isma'ili Shia militant movement that set up a religious state in al-Ahsa in Eastern Arabia in 899, under a dynasty founded by Abu Sa'id al-Jannabi. They revolted against both the Fatimid and Abbasid caliphates. In 930, under Abu Tahir al-Jannabi, they sacked Mecca, took the Black Stone, and later held it for ransom, which the Abbasids paid. For much of the 10th century they were the strongest force in the Persian Gulf, collecting tribute from the caliph in Baghdad and from Cairo.

entries_new.name: Münster rebellion
entries_new.founder: Bernhard Knipperdolling and John of Leiden
entries_new.laws: Compulsory polygamy under John of Leiden
entries_new.mechanism: A religious group won influence in a city, took its government and held it against a siege.
entries_new.story: Radical Anabaptists, a Christian sect, took the German city of Münster in February 1534, seized the city hall and installed Bernhard Knipperdolling as mayor. The expelled bishop, Franz von Waldeck, besieged the city. Its later leader John of Leiden took royal regalia and absolute power in what he called Zion. With at least three times as many marriageable women as men, he made polygamy compulsory and took sixteen wives. The besiegers took the city on 24 June 1535, and the leaders were captured.

entries_new.name: Slovak Soviet Republic
entries_new.mechanism: A communist government was declared in territory contested between Hungary and Czechoslovakia.
entries_new.story: The Slovak Soviet Republic was a short-lived communist state in southeastern Slovakia from 16 June to 7 July 1919, with its capital at Prešov. It was set up and led by the Czech journalist Antonín Janoušek, under the influence of the Hungarian Soviet Republic, and arose during fighting between Hungary and the Czechoslovak Army. It lasted about three weeks.

entries_new.name: Bremen Soviet Republic
entries_new.founder: Workers' and Soldiers' Council of Bremen
entries_new.mechanism: A workers' and soldiers' council replaced a city senate and ruled through councils.
entries_new.story: The Bremen Soviet Republic was an unrecognised revolutionary state in the German port city of Bremen. A Workers' and Soldiers' Council deposed the city's Senate on 10 November 1918, and the regime held power from 14 November, though it was not formally declared until 10 January 1919. On 4 February 1919, regular army troops and irregular Freikorps sent by the provisional government in Berlin occupied the city, breaking a disorganised resistance.

entries_new.name: Soviet Republic of Nargen
aka: Soviet Republic of Soldiers and Fortress-Builders of Nargen
entries_new.founder: Stepan Petrichenko and the garrison council
entries_new.mechanism: Sailors garrisoning an island fort declared it a republic and appointed commissars.
entries_new.story: Naissaar, or Nargen, is an island of 18.6 square km off Tallinn, Estonia, emptied of inhabitants in 1914 for a Russian naval fort with 80 to 90 sailors. After the October Revolution the sailors formed a council on 17 December 1917, elected Stepan Petrichenko chairman, and declared an independent Soviet republic with commissars, a draft constitution and the red-black flag. It meant to issue money. German forces occupied the island on 26 February 1918, the fleet evacuated most of the people, and the republic ended. Petrichenko later led the Kronstadt rebellion.

zones_new.name: Pirate bases that governed themselves
zones_new.who_owns: Whichever country holds the coast or island. On the high seas no country owns the water, and every country may seize a pirate ship there.

rules.cite: UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, Art. 100
rules.says: All states must cooperate as fully as possible to repress piracy on the high seas or anywhere outside any state's jurisdiction.

rules.cite: UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, Art. 101
rules.says: Piracy means illegal violence, detention or plunder committed for private ends by the crew or passengers of a private ship or aircraft, on the high seas or outside any state's jurisdiction. Knowingly helping to run a pirate ship counts too.

rules.cite: UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, Art. 103 and 104
rules.says: A ship is a pirate ship if those in control intend to use it for piracy or have used it and still control it. It may keep its nationality, depending on the law of its flag state.

rules.cite: UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, Art. 105
rules.says: On the high seas every state may seize a pirate ship and arrest those on board, and its courts may decide the penalties.

rules.cite: UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, Art. 106 and 107
rules.says: Only warships, military aircraft or marked government ships may make the seizure. A state that seizes without adequate grounds owes compensation to the ship's flag state.

zones_new.hook: Pirates have run ports for years at a time, but every country's navy may seize a pirate ship on the high seas, and the bases on record ended by force, surrender or sale.
zones_new.can_you_build: A base can be built only on someone's coast, and it depends on that government being weak or willing to look away. Raiding from it is a crime every state may punish on the high seas.
facts: Nassau: over 1,000 pirates and about 100 townspeople around 1715, ended by a governor in 1718.
Salé: a council of 12 to 16 ran the port from 1627 to 1668.
Tortuga: sold for 15,000 livres to a French company in 1664.
Libertalia: known only from a 1724 book, and modern scholars regard it as fiction.
Somalia: attempted hijackings fell from 237 in 2011 to 75 in 2012.

sources.t: Piracy off the coast of Somalia
UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, Part VII (text copy)
Legal Framework for the Repression of Piracy Under UNCLOS (United Nations)

zones_new.essay:
A pirate haven is a port or cove where pirates can repair ships, take on supplies, sell what they have stolen and avoid capture. These places existed where a government could not or would not enforce the law at sea. Some were set up by governments themselves, which paid privateers (private ships licensed to raid in wartime) to disrupt a rival's trade.

Some did run themselves for a time. Nassau, in the Bahamas, had lost its English government after attacks in 1703 and 1706. Pirates moved in from 1713 and followed a code under which crews voted on captains and shared loot. It was not a republic in any formal sense. Woodes Rogers arrived as royal governor in 1718 with a pardon, and nine men were executed that December. Salé, in Morocco, went further. Refugees from Spain expelled the sultan's governor in 1627 and elected their own through a council. An English diplomat negotiated a treaty with their ally, Dutch and French consuls later lived there, and the sultan ended its independence in 1668.

Other famous cases fall short of self-rule. On Tortuga, the source says the pirates never really controlled the island, and a buccaneer sold it to a French company in 1664. Port Royal stayed an English colony. Jean Lafitte's colony on Galveston flew Mexico's flag and carried forged licences from an imaginary nation, and he left in 1821 when a US Navy schooner came for him. Zheng Yi Sao's confederation had about 400 junks in 1805 and ended with a negotiated surrender and pardon in 1810. Libertalia, the best known pirate utopia, appears only in a 1724 book, and modern scholars treat it as fiction. The writer who coined the term pirate utopia, Peter Lamborn Wilson, admitted to adding a touch of fantasy.

The law now leaves little room. Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, every state may seize a pirate ship on the high seas, and its own courts may set the penalty. Piracy is defined by private ends, so robbery for profit qualifies whatever flag or code the crew claims. Inside a country's own coastal waters the same acts are armed robbery, and the coastal state is mainly responsible.

Somalia shows the modern version. After the navy dissolved around 1991, fishermen formed armed groups, and towns such as Eyl, Harardhere and Hobyo became bases. In June 2008, with the consent of Somalia's government, the UN Security Council let foreign navies enter Somali waters to pursue pirates. Attempted hijackings fell from 237 in 2011 to 75 in 2012. By 2010 Puntland's forces had pushed pirates out of Eyl. The Security Council mandate expired in March 2022, and hijackings were reported again in 2026.

odds.why: A camp on a weak coast can be set up, and raiding pays for a while. The law is the barrier: any navy may seize the ships. Nassau lasted about five years. Salé lasted about 41, with refugees and a large fleet, and treaties with outsiders. Recognition of a pirate base as a state has no modern example.

own.own_why: You would get a harbour, a code voted by crews and some years of income. Salé shows a council and treaties can follow. It falls short because a base lives on crimes every state may punish, so holding it for ten years depends on no navy deciding to come. Nassau fell to one governor and Eyl to one regional force.

zones_new.name: Taking a ship or settling after a mutiny
zones_new.who_owns: The ship stays under the law of its flag country, whoever is in control of it. Land the mutineers reach belongs to whichever country holds it or later claims it.

rules.cite: UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, Art. 102
rules.says: When the crew of a warship or government ship mutinies and takes control, piracy they commit is treated the same as piracy by a private ship.

A person commits an offence by seizing or taking control of a ship by force, threat or intimidation. Under Art. 6(4), a state party where the offender is found must establish jurisdiction if it does not extradite.

rules.cite: US Uniform Code of Military Justice, Art. 94 (10 USC 894)
rules.says: Refusing orders or making violence together with others, with intent to override lawful military authority, is mutiny. It can be punished by death or as a court-martial directs.
Mutiny covers acting together to overthrow or resist authority, or disobeying in a way that subverts discipline. The Human Rights Act 1998 ended the death penalty for it in the UK.

zones_new.hook: A crew can take a ship in minutes, but the ship keeps its flag, needs fuel and food from someone's port, and only Pitcairn shows mutineers lasting on land.
zones_new.can_you_build: A seized ship remains a stolen ship and needs a port to stay afloat, and most mutineers on record surrendered it or sought asylum within days or weeks. A settlement on land lasted only where nobody came looking, and Pitcairn became a British colony.
facts: Pitcairn: 9 mutineers settled in 1790, and 35 permanent residents lived there in 2023.
Potemkin: seized in June 1905 and given up in Romania by July.
Santa Maria: 24 rebels with Galvão held 600 passengers and 300 crew for 11 days in 1961.
Storozhevoy: 13 ships and 60 aircraft sent after one Soviet frigate in 1975.
Batavia: about 125 survivors murdered in 1629 before mutineers were tried and executed.

sources.t: UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, Part VII (text copy)
Piracy: A Modern Conspectus (US Naval Institute Proceedings, 1965)
IMO submission on universal jurisdiction, quoting the SUA Convention (UN Sixth Committee)

zones_new.essay:
A mutiny is a group refusing or overthrowing lawful command on a ship or in a military unit. Taking a ship looks like a way out of every country at once, since a ship can leave any coast. The record shows the ship stays tied to the world in two ways: it remains under the law of its flag, and it needs supplies.

Supplies usually decide it. The crew of the Russian battleship Potemkin killed seven officers in June 1905 and ran the ship by committee. Romania refused them coal and food, and gave them asylum only if they disarmed and handed the ship over. Two crew who seized the Columbia Eagle in 1970 sailed to Cambodia, which first granted asylum and later jailed them. Sailors on HMS Hermione in 1797 killed their officers and surrendered the ship to Spain.

A government comes after its ships quickly. Valery Sablin took the Soviet frigate Storozhevoy in November 1975 to broadcast a political message. Thirteen naval vessels and 60 warplanes went after it, and aircraft damaged its steering. Portuguese sailors who tried to leave the Tagus in 1936 were stopped by coastal guns.

Settling on land gives two kinds of result. On the Globe in 1824, Samuel Comstock wanted his own kingdom on Mili Atoll, and his fellow mutineers shot him. Jeronimus Cornelisz ruled the Batavia survivors by massacre in 1629, until a rescue ship came and he was executed. Pitcairn is the exception. Nine Bounty mutineers and their Tahitian companions burned the ship there in 1790. Passing ships ignored the island for years. It then became a British colony, by the islanders' count in 1838. It had 35 residents in 2023, and a high-profile criminal trial took place there in 2004.

The legal position depends on what the takers are after. The law of the sea treats a mutinied warship that commits piracy as a private ship. The older treaty language made the same point, as a 1965 US naval article records. Piracy needs private ends, and politics can fall outside it. When Henrique Galvão took the liner Santa Maria in 1961, intending to reach Angola and set up a rebel government, US legal experts could not support a finding of piracy, and the United States treated him as an insurgent. Brazil gave him asylum. The 1988 SUA Convention makes seizing a ship by force an offence on international voyages, and a state party must be able to try a suspect found on its soil if it does not extradite. The US Supreme Court freed the Amistad captives, who had seized their ship, in 1841.

Some mutinies changed a country and took no territory. The sailors of Kiel took their city through councils in November 1918, and the German monarchy fell within days. The Brazilian sailors of 1910 won a law ending the lash.

odds.why: Taking a ship has often worked for days. Law and money fail next: the seizure is a crime under military law and the SUA Convention, the ship stays flagged to its old state, and every port is someone's. Pitcairn held only because no one looked, and it joined Britain.

own.own_why: You would get a ship and a committee for days or weeks, or, at best, a remote island as Pitcairn's settlers did. It falls short because a ship needs ports that answer to governments, and navies pursue their own hulls. Pitcairn's settlers stayed apart only until found, and the island is now a British territory.

zones_new.name: Uprisings that held a city or region under their own rule
zones_new.who_owns: The existing country, in law, until it loses a war or agrees to let go. An uprising controls ground in fact and holds no title to it.

rules.says: In an armed conflict inside one country, each side must at least treat non-fighters humanely, with no murder or torture, and care for the wounded. Applying these rules does not change the legal status of either side.

rules.cite: US Uniform Code of Military Justice, Art. 94 (10 USC 894)
rules.says: Service members who act together with intent to overthrow or destroy lawful civil authority commit sedition, punishable by death or as a court-martial directs.

rules.cite: UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, Art. 101
rules.says: Piracy requires private ends. A US naval study of the 1961 Santa Maria case shows political seizures at sea can fall outside it and be treated as insurgency.

zones_new.hook: People in revolt have held Paris for 71 days and a Brazilian settlement for 89 years, and most such governments ended when an army came.
zones_new.can_you_build: An uprising can take a city quickly if the army or police are divided or absent, but it comes from people already living there, and it holds only while it can beat the army. No law protects the result, and Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions gives it no status.
facts: Paris 1871: 71 days and a council of 92, with 10,000 to 15,000 Communards killed, by estimates.
Limerick 1919: two weeks and its own strike money.
Gwangju 1980: government count 165 dead, later estimates about 600 to 2,300.
Hungary 1919: about 60% of the former territory at the start, gone by August.

sources.t: Common Article 3 to the Geneva Conventions (Crimes of War)
Piracy: A Modern Conspectus (US Naval Institute Proceedings, 1965)

zones_new.essay:
An uprising takes the opposite route from most attempts in this collection. Nobody looks for empty land. People already living in a place stop obeying their government and run it themselves, usually at a moment when that government has been weakened by a war or a revolution. Paris rose in 1871 after France's defeat by Prussia. Limerick's strike committee acted at the start of the Irish War of Independence, and Munich's revolutionaries during the German revolution of 1918 to 1919. Catalonia's unions took control during the Spanish Civil War.

Many set up working institutions fast. The Paris Commune held elections within eight days, choosing a council of 92, and separated church and state. Limerick printed money that local businesses accepted. In Manchuria, Korean refugees ran village assemblies, banks and schools. Makhno's region in Ukraine held congresses of peasants and workers. The Republic of Ezo held Japan's first election in 1869, limited to samurai, and approached foreign legations for recognition.

Most lasted weeks. Limerick lasted 14 days, Strandzha about a month, Bavaria under a month, Kronstadt 16 days, Canton a short time at a cost of more than 5,700 dead. Paris lasted 71 days. The Hungarian Soviet Republic held about 60% of the former territory and lost it in less than five months. Endings tended to be violent, and the figures are disputed. Estimates for Paris run from 10,000 to 15,000 Communards killed, with one unconfirmed figure of 20,000. In Gwangju the government claimed 165 dead, and scholars now estimate about 600 to 2,300.

The longer cases held remote or difficult ground, or fought for land itself. Palmares, a settlement of escaped slaves and others in Brazil, grew from 1605 and beat six Portuguese expeditions in the 1680s before an army ended it in 1694. Its size is disputed, at about 11,000 or about 20,000. Zapata's forces, based in Morelos, fought from 1911 to 1920, and his successor negotiated peace after Carranza fell. The Zanj revolt in Iraq lasted 14 years, and the Sicilian slaves under Eunus lasted three and had a king.

Some were not free of the state at all. The Shanghai People's Commune of 1967 came from a coup backed by national leaders, and it collapsed within 18 days after Mao withdrew his support. The Council of Aragon was dissolved by the republican government it served, under Communist pressure.

The law gives little. Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions sets minimum rules for civil wars, and it says plainly that those rules do not change the legal status of either side. Rebels gain protection for the wounded and for fighters who lay down their arms, and no title to land. Service members who join can face sedition charges under military law. Some movements gained in defeat: the Kronstadt crisis sped up the New Economic Policy, though the rebels' demands were not met.

odds.why: Taking a city has happened often where a war or revolution had weakened the state. No law protects it, money comes from what is seized or printed, and few held past a year. Palmares and Morelos held longer on difficult ground, and each had a population with its own reason to fight.

own.own_why: You would get a city or valley, your own councils and perhaps your own money, for weeks in most cases on record. Outsiders with no local people have almost nothing to rise with, so the private figure is very low. An existing people does better, as Palmares and Morelos show, but it falls short of ten years free of override because the state keeps its legal claim and most uprisings ended when its army returned.
